da-2026-da-17.approach: Find the critical points from $f'(x)=3x(x-2)$, evaluate $f$ there and at the closed end $x=3$ (the end $x=-1$ is excluded), and factor out the obvious root $x=1$ to locate every root. One small value table settles all four options.
concepts: Global extrema on a half-open interval
da-2026-da-17.given: $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+2$ on $(-1,3]$ — the left end $-1$ is **open** (not in the domain), the right end $3$ is **closed**.

steps.title: Critical points
steps.body: $$f'(x)=3x^2-6x=3x(x-2)=0 \;\Rightarrow\; x=0 \text{ or } x=2,$$ both inside $(-1,3]$. With $f''(x)=6x-6$: $f''(0)=-6<0$ (local max) and $f''(2)=6>0$ (local min). Sign of $f'$: positive on $(-1,0)$, negative on $(0,2)$, positive on $(2,3]$.

steps.title: Values at the candidates
steps.body:
- $f(0)=0-0+2=2$
- $f(2)=8-12+2=-2$
- $f(3)=27-27+2=2$ (closed end, so it counts)
- $x\to -1^+$: $f(x)\to -1-3+2=-2$, but $x=-1$ is not in the domain, so the value $-2$ is **not attained** there.

steps.title: Maximum and minimum
steps.body:
**Maximum value** $=2$, reached at $x=0$ **and** at $x=3$ — so "maximum at 0 only" is false.

**Minimum value** $=-2$. On $(-1,0]$, $f$ is strictly increasing from values above $-2$ (the limit $-2$ at $-1$ is never reached), so $f>-2$ there; on $[0,3]$ the only place $f=-2$ is $x=2$. Hence the minimum is attained **at 2 only** — (B) true.

scene.caption: max 2 at x = 0 and x = 3; min −2 only at x = 2

steps.title: Roots
steps.body:
$f(1)=1-3+2=0$, so $x=1$ is a root — (D) true. Dividing by $(x-1)$:
$$x^3-3x^2+2=(x-1)(x^2-2x-2),\qquad x^2-2x-2=0 \Rightarrow x=1\pm\sqrt3.$$
Roots: $1-\sqrt3\approx-0.732$, $1$, $1+\sqrt3\approx2.732$. Only $-0.732$ lies in $[-0.9,0]$, so there is **exactly one** root there — (A) false.

answer.value: **(B) and (D)** — the minimum is attained only at $x=2$, and $x=1$ is a root

optionAnalysis.reason: $f$ is strictly increasing on $[-0.9,0]$ ($f'>0$ for $x<0$) and goes from $f(-0.9)=-1.159$ to $f(0)=2$: exactly **one** root ($1-\sqrt3\approx-0.732$), not two.
The minimum value $-2$ is attained only at $x=2$; near $x=-1$ the function approaches $-2$ but $-1$ is excluded from the domain.
The maximum value $2$ is attained at $x=0$ and also at the closed end $x=3$ ($f(3)=2$), so "only" fails.

da-2026-da-17.shortcut: Sum of coefficients $1-3+2=0$ instantly gives the root $x=1$. Then just compare $f(0)=2$, $f(2)=-2$, $f(3)=2$ and remember that the open end $-1$ cannot host an extremum.
pitfalls: Ignoring the closed end $x=3$, where $f(3)=2$ ties the local maximum — this makes (C) look true.
Treating $f(-1)=-2$ as attained: $-1$ is excluded, so the minimum is still at 2 only.
Counting $1+\sqrt3$ or $1$ as roots in $[-0.9,0]$.
da-2026-da-17.verification: Sign check for (A): $f(-0.9)=-0.729-2.43+2=-1.159<0$ and $f(0)=2>0$ with $f$ monotonic in between ⇒ one root. Product of roots $(1-\sqrt3)(1)(1+\sqrt3)=1-3=-2=-\tfrac{2}{1}$ ✓ (matches $-d/a$).

da-2026-da-18.approach: Both distributions are symmetric about 0, so their CDFs agree at 0. The $t_1$ (Cauchy) density is lower at the centre and has heavier tails: it lies **below** the normal density on $(-c,c)$ and **above** it for $\lvert y\rvert>c$. That orders the tail areas, and symmetry gives the other side.

steps.title: Peak heights: option (D)
steps.body: $g(0)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\approx0.3989$ and $h(0)=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\approx0.3183$. They differ, so (D) is false; the normal is taller at the centre.

steps.title: Symmetry: option (A)
steps.body: Both densities are even functions, so half the mass lies on each side of 0: $G(0)=H(0)=\tfrac12$. (A) is true.

steps.title: Where the densities cross
steps.body: Ratio $\dfrac{g(y)}{h(y)}=\sqrt{\tfrac{\pi}{2}}\,(1+y^2)\,e^{-y^2/2}$. At $y=0$ it is $\sqrt{\pi/2}\approx1.25>1$. With $u=y^2$, $\dfrac{d}{du}\big[(1+u)e^{-u/2}\big]=\tfrac12(1-u)e^{-u/2}$: the ratio rises until $u=1$ and then falls to $0$, so it crosses $1$ exactly once, at $c\approx1.85$. Hence $g>h$ on $(-c,c)$ and $h>g$ for $\lvert y\rvert>c$ — the $t_1$ tails are heavier.

steps.title: Left tail: option (C)
steps.body: $$G(-c)=\int_{-\infty}^{-c}g(t)\,dt<\int_{-\infty}^{-c}h(t)\,dt=H(-c),$$ because $h>g$ on the whole range $(-\infty,-c)$. Numerically $G(-1.85)\approx0.032$ while $H(-1.85)=\tfrac12-\tfrac{\arctan 1.85}{\pi}\approx0.158$. (C) is true.

steps.title: Right side: option (B)
steps.body:
By symmetry $G(c)=1-G(-c)$ and $H(c)=1-H(-c)$. Since $G(-c)<H(-c)$,
$$G(c)=1-G(-c)>1-H(-c)=H(c).$$ The inequality in (B) is reversed, so (B) is false.

optionAnalysis.reason: Both distributions are symmetric about 0, so each CDF equals $\tfrac12$ at 0.
$G(c)=1-G(-c)>1-H(-c)=H(c)$: the normal has *more* mass below $c$ because it has less in the right tail.
For $t<-c$ the Cauchy density exceeds the normal one, so the left-tail area $H(-c)$ is larger.
$g(0)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}\approx0.399\neq h(0)=1/\pi\approx0.318$.

da-2026-da-18.shortcut: Heavy tails ⇒ more probability beyond $\pm c$: $H(-c)>G(-c)$ and, mirrored, $H(c)<G(c)$. Symmetry ⇒ $G(0)=H(0)=\tfrac12$.
pitfalls: Assuming the heavier-tailed distribution also has the larger CDF at $+c$ — on the right side the inequality flips.
Thinking two symmetric densities must have the same peak height.

da-2026-da-19.approach: One SGD step is $w \leftarrow w-\eta\,\dfrac{\partial f_w(x)}{\partial w}$ evaluated on the current input. For $f_w(x)=wx$ the gradient with respect to $w$ is simply $x$, so the step is $\eta x$.
concepts: Gradient with respect to the parameter

steps.title: Gradient with respect to w
steps.body: $$\frac{\partial f_w(x)}{\partial w}=\frac{\partial (wx)}{\partial w}=x=10.00.$$

steps.title: Read off the answer
steps.body: The step moved $w$ by $-\eta x=-1.00$, against the gradient, as descent requires. Rounded to two decimals, $w$ at the end of iteration $(i+1)$ is **9.00**, inside the official range $8.90$ to $9.10$.

da-2026-da-19.shortcut: Linear objective ⇒ constant gradient $x$: the new weight is $w-\eta x=10-1=9$.
pitfalls: Adding the step ($w+\eta x=11$) — gradient *descent* moves against the gradient.
Differentiating with respect to $x$ instead of $w$: here it gives the same number only because $w=x=10$.
da-2026-da-19.verification: The objective decreases as required: before the step $f=10\times10=100$, after it $f=9\times10=90<100$.

da-2026-da-20.approach: Minimax back-up from the leaves: each MIN node takes the minimum of its three terminal values, then MAX takes the maximum of those backed-up values. The best strategy is the edge leading to that maximum.
da-2026-da-20.given:
| MAX strategy | MIN strategy 1 | MIN strategy 2 | MIN strategy 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8 | 6 | −1 |
| 2 | 1 | 5 | 7 |
| 3 | −4 | −3 | −12 |

steps.title: MIN node after MAX strategy 1
steps.body: MIN picks the smallest utility: $\min(8,6,-1)=-1$. Even though $8$ is the best leaf in the whole tree, MIN will never let MAX reach it.

steps.title: MIN node after MAX strategy 2
steps.body: MIN compares its three replies and picks the smallest: $\min(1,5,7)=1$ (its strategy 1). This is the best guaranteed value so far for MAX, since $1>-1$.

steps.title: MIN node after MAX strategy 3
steps.body: All three leaves are negative and MIN picks the smallest: $\min(-4,-3,-12)=-12$ (its strategy 3).

steps.title: MAX chooses at the root
steps.body: $\max(-1,\,1,\,-12)=1$, obtained through strategy **2**. With optimal play MAX moves along edge 2, MIN replies with its strategy 1, and the game value is $1$.

da-2026-da-20.shortcut: Read off each MIN group's smallest leaf (−1, 1, −12) and pick the group with the largest of these: the middle one, strategy 2.
pitfalls: Choosing strategy 1 because it contains the largest leaf (8) — MIN would answer with −1.
Answering the game value (1) instead of the strategy number (2); here they differ.
Taking the average of each group (expectimax) instead of the minimum.
da-2026-da-20.verification: Alpha–beta gives the same result: after the first subtree α = −1; the second subtree returns 1, so α = 1; in the third subtree the first leaf −4 ≤ α already prunes the rest, confirming MAX prefers strategy 2.

da-2026-da-21.approach: Each recursive step makes one 3-way comparison with the middle element and then continues on one side. In the worst case it always keeps the **larger** side, of size $\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ from a range of size $m$. Count the non-empty ranges until the range becomes empty: that count is $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1$.

steps.title: What one step does
steps.body: For a range of $m$ elements, the middle element is compared with $y$ (one comparison). If $y$ is not equal, the remaining $m-1$ elements split into two sides of sizes $\lceil (m-1)/2\rceil$ and $\lfloor (m-1)/2\rfloor$. The larger is $\lceil (m-1)/2\rceil=\lfloor m/2\rfloor$, so the worst case continues with $\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ elements.

steps.title: Follow the worst-case sizes
steps.body: $$1000\to500\to250\to125\to62\to31\to15\to7\to3\to1\to0$$ Every non-empty range costs one comparison: the ranges of size $1000, 500, 250, 125, 62, 31, 15, 7, 3, 1$ give **10** comparisons. When the range is empty the search stops ("not found") without comparing.

scene.caption: 10 comparisons, then the range is empty

steps.title: Same result by the formula
steps.body: Maximum comparisons $=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil$. Since $2^9=512\le1000<1024=2^{10}$, $\lfloor\log_2 1000\rfloor=9$, giving $9+1=10$.

pitfalls: Counting the final empty-range call as a comparison (answer 11).
Writing $\log_2 1000\approx9.97$ and truncating to 9.
Counting "equal?" and "less than?" as two separate comparisons — the question defines one 3-way comparison per step.
da-2026-da-21.verification: Small case: $n=3$ (with $2^1\le3<2^2$) needs at most $\lfloor\log_2 3\rfloor+1=2$ comparisons: compare the middle, then the single remaining element on the chosen side, then the range is empty ✓.

da-2026-da-22.approach: In a B+ tree only the **leaves** store data-record pointers; a non-leaf node with $p$ node pointers stores $p-1$ search keys. So find the largest $p$ with $10p+11(p-1)\le4096$.
da-2026-da-22.given:
| Item | Size |
|---|---|
| Node (block) | 4096 B |
| Node pointer | 10 B |
| Search key | 11 B |
| Data record pointer | 12 B (leaves only) |

steps.title: Layout of a non-leaf node
steps.body: A non-leaf node with $p$ node pointers interleaves them with $p-1$ keys: $P_1\,K_1\,P_2\,K_2\cdots K_{p-1}\,P_p$. No data-record pointers appear in internal nodes of a B+ tree. Size: $$10p+11(p-1)\le4096.$$

steps.title: Solve for p
steps.body: $$10p+11p-11\le4096 \;\Rightarrow\; 21p\le4107 \;\Rightarrow\; p\le\frac{4107}{21}=195.57\ldots$$ so $p=195$.

steps.title: Check the boundary
steps.body:
- $p=195$: $195\times10+194\times11=1950+2134=4084\le4096$ ✓ (12 bytes spare)
- $p=196$: $196\times10+195\times11=1960+2145=4105>4096$ ✗

Maximum number of node pointers in a non-leaf node $=$ **195**.

pitfalls: Including data-record pointers in internal nodes (B-tree formula): $10p+(11+12)(p-1)\le4096$ gives $124$ — wrong for a B+ tree.
Using the leaf-node formula: $(11+12)k+10\le4096$ gives $k=177$ keys per leaf, which answers a different question.
da-2026-da-22.verification: Boundary check above: 195 pointers fit (4084 B) and 196 do not (4105 B).

da-2026-da-23.approach: $f(f(n))=n$ means $f$ is an **involution**: in its cycle decomposition every cycle has length 1 or 2. Count the bijections by how many disjoint swaps (2-cycles) they contain.

steps.title: Why only fixed points and swaps
steps.body: If $f$ had a cycle $a\to b\to c\to\cdots$ of length $\ge3$, then $f(f(a))=c\neq a$. With a 2-cycle $a\leftrightarrow b$: $f(f(a))=f(b)=a$ ✓; with a fixed point $f(a)=a$ ✓. So $f$ is a product of disjoint transpositions.

steps.title: Zero or one swap
steps.body:
- No swap: the identity — $1$ map.
- Exactly one swap: choose the pair, $\binom42=6$ maps; the other two elements are fixed.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: Add the three disjoint cases (0, 1 or 2 swaps): $$1+6+3=10.$$

pitfalls: Forgetting the identity map (answer 9).
Counting the two-swap maps as $\binom42\binom22=6$ — each pairing is counted twice; divide by $2!$ to get 3.
Answering $4!=24$ (all bijections) — most of them are not their own inverse.
da-2026-da-23.verification: The recurrence in the shortcut is an independent count: element $n$ is either fixed ($a(n-1)$ ways) or swapped with one of the other $n-1$ elements ($a(n-2)$ ways each) — it also gives 10.

da-2026-da-24.approach: The exponential distribution is **memoryless**: $P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)$. With $s=t=5$ the answer is $P(X>5)=0.35$ directly — no need to find $\lambda$.

steps.title: Use the survival function
steps.body:
With mean $\lambda$, $P(X>t)=e^{-t/\lambda}$. So
$$\frac{e^{-10/\lambda}}{e^{-5/\lambda}}=e^{-5/\lambda}=P(X>5)=0.35.$$
(Equivalently $P(X>10)=\big(e^{-5/\lambda}\big)^2=0.35^2=0.1225$ and $0.1225/0.35=0.35$.)

steps.title: Interpret: memorylessness
steps.body: The ratio did not depend on $\lambda$ at all: in general $P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=e^{-t/\lambda}=P(X>t)$. With $s=5$, $t=5$ the answer is $P(X>5)=$ **0.35**.

da-2026-da-24.shortcut: Memorylessness: having survived 5 units, the chance of surviving 5 more equals the original chance of surviving 5, i.e. 0.35.
pitfalls: Reporting $P(X>10)=0.1225$ instead of the conditional probability.
Worrying whether $\lambda$ is the mean or the rate: the answer does not depend on the parameterisation.

da-2026-da-25.approach: The term $2^{-i}3^{-j}$ factorises into a function of $i$ times a function of $j$, and all terms are positive, so the double series equals the **product of two geometric series**.

steps.title: Separate the sums
steps.body: $$\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}2^{-i}3^{-j}=\Big(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}2^{-i}\Big)\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}3^{-j}\Big).$$

steps.title: Sum over i (starts at 0)
steps.body: $$\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\Big(\tfrac12\Big)^i=\frac{1}{1-\tfrac12}=2.$$

steps.title: Sum over j (starts at 1)
steps.body: $$\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\Big(\tfrac13\Big)^j=\frac{\tfrac13}{1-\tfrac13}=\frac{1/3}{2/3}=\frac12.$$

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body: $$2\times\frac12=1.$$

pitfalls: Starting $j$ at 0: $\sum_{j\ge0}3^{-j}=\tfrac32$ gives $3$.
Starting $i$ at 1: $\sum_{i\ge1}2^{-i}=1$ gives $\tfrac12$.
da-2026-da-25.verification: Partial sum check: terms with $i\le3$, $j\le3$ give $(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\tfrac18)(\tfrac13+\tfrac19+\tfrac1{27})=1.875\times0.4815\approx0.903$, approaching 1 from below ✓.

da-2026-da-26.approach: Agglomerative clustering starts with singletons and first merges the closest pair of points — whatever the linkage. So compute all six Manhattan (L1) distances and take the minimum.

steps.title: Distances from P1
steps.body:
$d(P_1,P_2)=\lvert2-3\rvert+\lvert3-1\rvert+\lvert-1-1\rvert=1+2+2=5$

$d(P_1,P_3)=\lvert2-5\rvert+\lvert3+2\rvert+\lvert-1-3\rvert=3+5+4=12$

$d(P_1,P_4)=\lvert2-3\rvert+\lvert3-3\rvert+\lvert-1-3\rvert=1+0+4=5$

steps.title: Remaining pairs
steps.body:
$d(P_2,P_3)=\lvert3-5\rvert+\lvert1+2\rvert+\lvert1-3\rvert=2+3+2=7$

$d(P_2,P_4)=\lvert3-3\rvert+\lvert1-3\rvert+\lvert1-3\rvert=0+2+2=4$

$d(P_3,P_4)=\lvert5-3\rvert+\lvert-2-3\rvert+\lvert3-3\rvert=2+5+0=7$

steps.title: Merge the closest pair
steps.body: Smallest distance: $\min\{5,12,5,7,4,7\}=4$ for $(P_2,P_4)$. They are merged first — option (D).

scene.caption: min distance 4 → merge P2 and P4

optionAnalysis.reason: $d(P_1,P_2)=5>4$ (tied with $P_1,P_4$, but neither is the minimum).
$d(P_2,P_4)=0+2+2=4$, the smallest of the six distances.

da-2026-da-26.shortcut: P2 and P4 share x = 3 and differ by 2 in each of y and z (total 4); every other pair differs by at least 5.
pitfalls: Using Euclidean distance out of habit — here it happens to pick the same pair, but in general L1 and L2 orderings can differ.
Forgetting absolute values on negative coordinate differences (e.g. $-1-1=-2$ must count as 2).
da-2026-da-26.verification: Euclidean cross-check: $d_2(P_2,P_4)=\sqrt{0+4+4}\approx2.83$ is also the smallest ($d_2(P_1,P_2)=3$), consistent with merging P2 and P4.

da-2026-da-27.approach: Recall what Ridge is: least squares plus an $L_2$ penalty, $\min_w \sum_i (y_i-w^\top x_i)^2+\lambda\lVert w\rVert_2^2$. The penalty shrinks all weights toward zero, trading a little bias for lower variance. Check each statement against that.

steps.title: The Ridge objective
steps.body: $$J(w)=\sum_{i}(y_i-w^\top x_i)^2+\lambda\lVert w\rVert_2^2,\qquad \lambda>0.$$ The penalty is the **squared $L_2$ norm**. It pulls every weight toward 0 (larger weights are punished more) but almost never makes a weight exactly 0.

steps.title: What the penalty is for
steps.body: It fights **overfitting**: a model that fits the training data very well but generalises poorly to test data. Shrinking the weights makes the fitted function less sensitive to the particular training sample, which **reduces variance**. The price is that the estimates are pulled away from the least-squares solution, which **increases bias**. This is exactly statement (D).

steps.title: Reject the other statements
steps.body:
- (A) describes the opposite situation (good on test, poor on training); regularisation guards against good-on-training, poor-on-test.
- (B) $L_1$ is the Lasso penalty; Ridge uses $L_2$.
- (C) Ridge shrinks magnitudes regardless of sign; it neither targets negative weights nor reduces the number of parameters.

answer.value: **(D)** — the regularizer may increase bias but reduces variance

optionAnalysis.reason: Reversed: regularisation guards against overfitting — doing well on the training data but poorly on the test data.
Ridge uses the (squared) $L_2$ norm; the $L_1$ norm is the Lasso penalty.
The penalty depends on $w_j^2$, so the sign of a weight is irrelevant; Ridge shrinks all weights and does not reduce the parameter count.
Shrinkage introduces bias but lowers the variance of the predictions — the bias–variance trade-off that Ridge exploits.

da-2026-da-27.shortcut: Ridge = L2 = shrink, not select; regularisation = accept bias to cut variance. Only (D) fits.
pitfalls: Mixing up Ridge ($L_2$) with Lasso ($L_1$).
Reading (A) quickly — it swaps "training" and "test".
da-2026-da-27.verification: Closed form $\hat w=(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y$: as $\lambda$ grows, $\hat w\to0$ (more bias, less variance); at $\lambda=0$ it is ordinary least squares (unbiased, highest variance). This confirms (D).

da-2026-da-28.approach: Translate the sentence first: "a creative person succeeds if disciplined and does not succeed otherwise" says that **for a creative person**, success holds exactly when discipline holds: $C\Rightarrow(S\Leftrightarrow D)$. Then test each statement for equivalence with that, using simplification and an 8-row truth table.

steps.title: Formalise the sentence
steps.body: For creative people: disciplined ⇒ succeed, and not disciplined ⇒ not succeed, i.e. $S\Leftrightarrow D$. Nothing is said about non-creative people. So the intended meaning is $$K\;=\;C\Rightarrow(S\Leftrightarrow D),$$ which is exactly statement (ii).

steps.title: Statement (i): $Cland SLeftrightarrow D$
steps.body: It also forces $D\Rightarrow C\land S$: every disciplined person must be creative and succeed. Rows $C=0, D=1$ satisfy $K$ (the sentence says nothing about non-creative people) but make (i) false. So (i) is **not** equivalent.

steps.title: Statement (iii) simplifies to $C$
steps.body:
$$(D\Rightarrow S)\lor
eg S=
eg D\lor S\lor
eg S=	op,$$ so (iii) is $C\Leftrightarrow	op\equiv C$ — "everyone is creative". It disagrees with $K$ whenever $C=0$, and is true in rows $C=1$ where $S
eq D$ (where $K$ is false). Not equivalent.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Only (ii) captures the sentence — option (B).

(ii) $C\Rightarrow(S\Leftrightarrow D)$ is the literal translation: for creative people, success exactly when disciplined.
(iii) reduces to just $C$ because $(D\Rightarrow S)\lor\neg S$ is a tautology.
(iii) ≡ $C$ says nothing about success or discipline, and (ii) — which is correct — is excluded.

da-2026-da-28.shortcut: "If creative, then (succeed iff disciplined)" is (ii) verbatim. Spot that $(D\Rightarrow S)\lor\neg S$ is a tautology to kill (iii) at once.
pitfalls: Reading (i) as "creative and disciplined ⇒ succeed": the biconditional with $D$ also requires every disciplined person to be creative.
Not simplifying (iii) — it collapses to $C$.

da-2026-da-29.approach: Let $C(n)$ be the number of activations made by mystery(n), including itself. A base call ($n\le0$) is 1 activation; otherwise $C(n)=1+C(n-1)+C(n-2)$. Note that mystery(1) is **not** a base case — it calls mystery(0) and mystery(-1).
concepts: Activation records on the call stack

steps.title: Base cases
steps.body: Any call with $n\le0$ returns 1 immediately: $C(0)=C(-1)=1$.

steps.title: n = 1 is recursive
steps.body: $1>0$, so mystery(1) calls mystery(0) and mystery(-1): $$C(1)=1+C(0)+C(-1)=1+1+1=3.$$

steps.title: The initial call
steps.body: $$C(4)=1+C(3)+C(2)=1+9+5=15.$$ The recursion tree has **15** nodes, each pushed on the stack once — option (C).

optionAnalysis.reason: Counts each distinct argument 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 once, as memoisation would; without memoisation every call is a new activation (and m(−1) is called too).
Treats $n\le1$ as the base case (Fibonacci-style): $C(1)=1$ gives $C(2)=3$, $C(3)=5$, $C(4)=9$. But mystery(1) recurses since $1>0$.
Overcount: the recursion tree has exactly 15 nodes and each activation is pushed once (9 in the m(3) subtree + 5 in the m(2) subtree + the initial call); 17 is not reachable from the recurrence.

da-2026-da-29.shortcut: $C(n)+1$ obeys the Fibonacci rule: $C(n)+1=(C(n-1)+1)+(C(n-2)+1)$ with starting values $2, 2$. Sequence $2,2,4,6,10,16$ for $n=-1..4$, so $C(4)=16-1=15$.
pitfalls: Assuming mystery(1) is a base case — the condition is n <= 0, so mystery(1) makes two more calls.
Counting only distinct arguments instead of every activation.
da-2026-da-29.verification: Count the tree directly: subtree of m(3) has 9 nodes, subtree of m(2) has 5, plus the root: 9 + 5 + 1 = 15. (The value returned, mystery(4) = 8, is irrelevant to the count.)
